_comment: Installations that are NOT live, and why. Read by `.github/scripts/lock-pinned-digests.py`
(AXIS 3) — MeshWeaver#3438 / #3858.
🚨 THIS FILE IS NOT THE ROSTER. The deployment overlays are: every `Hosting__Deployment:` a
`values*.yaml` in the fleet declares is an installation the protection run EXPECTS to answer
`/api/version`. An installation that is missing from THIS file is therefore LIVE, and a live
installation that does not answer makes the run INCOMPLETE and refuses the unlock arm. So
forgetting an entry here is always the stricter mistake, never the looser one — which is the
only direction a hand-maintained file is allowed to fail in.
What it exists for is the distinction #3858 asks for in as many words: *retirement is
explicit and auditable; a temporarily unavailable portal is not treated as retired*. A portal
that is down and a portal that was decommissioned are the same silence, and only one of them
may have its images collected. Silence is unavailability. A line here is retirement.
`state` is one of: live | not-installed | retired. Anything else is a RED, as is a non-live
entry with no `reason`, as is an entry naming an installation no overlay declares (a stale
exemption hides the next one).
🚨 `registries` (below) ACCOUNTS FOR EVERY REGISTRY THE FLEET'S OVERLAYS NAME, and the UNIT
is the registry rather than the installation — deliberately. A per-instance field answers
'is this one out of scope' and can never answer 'is every registry the fleet pins in
accounted for': an installation pinning its declared registry AND a second undeclared one
would pass it with half its running set unnamed. A per-instance `registry` key is therefore
REFUSED, so a stale one cannot sit there looking like a declaration.
Two dispositions, and the difference is load-bearing. 🚨 BOTH ARE ABOUT WHAT THE FLEET
PULLS — which is what every axis reads them for: `foreign_registries` comes off deployment
overlays, and the question asked is whether an installation's RUNNING SET is accounted for.
What the fleet PUSHES to a host is a separate fact with a separate field (`publishes`,
below), because a host can be MIXED and `ghcr.io` is:
fleet-unlockable  serves OUR images and this lane cannot lock them. An installation running
from one is out of THIS lane's scope — still live, still expected to
answer, still counted, and printed on its own line saying protection there
is UNVERIFIED. It never claims the other registry protects anything.
third-party       the images are somebody else's and were never ours to protect. Reported,
never a blocker.
An UNDECLARED host is a BLOCKER wherever it appears — including on an installation that also
pins in this ACR, where half its running set would otherwise be protected and half not while
the run reported success.
🚨 `retention` (on every registry entry) IS THE SECOND QUESTION ASKED OF THE SAME UNIT, and
it is REQUIRED. `disposition` says whether this lane can lock a registry; it says nothing
about whether anything DELETES from it, and for a year the answer to the second question for
cr.meshweaver.cloud was 'established by nothing' (MeshWeaver#4230). The table is the unit that
can be shown COMPLETE, so a registry entering the fleet now has to answer both. Three rules:
nothing-deletes        no deleter exists, and none may be added before a cleanup can derive
a protected set. Requires `deleters` — every mechanism that COULD
delete, each with `present` and a `verdict` — and AT LEAST ONE must
be `present: true`: an enumeration in which nothing is present is an
enumeration that inspected nothing, which reads exactly like a clean
one. Requires `chart`, the committed source the gate re-derives the
deleters FROM, and `deleteGrantedTo`, the principal the registry's
ACL may grant the `delete` action to — one verdict here rests on that
ACL and on nothing else, so the gate re-reads it too.
🚨 `present` HAS THREE STATES, and the third is why this block exists:
true (measured, and it IS there), false (measured, and it is not) and
"unverified" (NOBODY COULD LOOK). Filing an unknown as `false` lets a
declaration read as fully measured over an open question — the
not-checked-spelled-as-clean confusion this whole family is made of.
An "unverified" row must name `verifiedBy` (what would answer it), it
is PRINTED on its own line on every run whatever the verdict, and
`cleanupAuthorized` — the record's own statement that deleting here
would be safe — may NOT be true while one stands. That is what the
unknown blocks: the ACT, not the gate. A check that is red until
somebody reads an Azure storage account is a check nobody reads.
derived-protected-set  a cleanup exists and deletes only the complement of a DERIVED set.
Requires `protectedSet.axes`, and every axis must declare
`onIncomplete: "refuse"` — on a registry with no lock an incomplete
derivation DELETES what it could not see, in the same act.
Requires `cleanup` — the job's `kind`, `repository`, `manual` and
`runsAs`, which must equal `deleteGrantedTo` (MeshWeaver#7530). It
is then held to EVERYTHING `nothing-deletes` is held to — the
`deleters` enumeration, the chart, the ACL and the deleter sweep —
because the day a cleanup exists is the day a second, unnamed
deleter matters most. Every `present: true` row is either the named
cleanup (`governedBy: <cleanup.kind>`) or a declared
`maintenance.<key>` timer, and at least one row is the cleanup.
`cleanupAuthorized: false` must say what it waits for in
`authorizationBlockedBy`; `true` may list nothing there.
not-ours               third-party; nothing of ours is stored there, so there is nothing to
protect. May NOT carry `deleters` — enumerating somebody else's
deleters would read as a verdict about our artifacts.
out-of-estate          our images live there and the registry is in an ESTATE outside this
fleet's reach — a different subscription, a credential this lane does
not hold — so what deletes from it is decided there. Requires
`estate` (whose decision it is, and where that decision lives) and
`cleanupAuthorized: false`, and may NOT carry `deleters`: we cannot
measure somebody else's mechanisms from a committed file, and a list
here would be a verdict about OUR artifacts resting on nothing.
🚨 IT IS NOT A TRAPDOOR OUT OF `nothing-deletes`, and the refusal is
DERIVED rather than declared: a host this fleet's own publishing
lanes push to may never take this rule — which is precisely
cr.meshweaver.cloud and meshweaver.azurecr.io, the two where it would
have mattered — and a run whose push-target derivation cannot be
trusted refuses the rule instead of allowing it. Every run PRINTS the
host on its own line saying this record measures nothing about it,
because 'not ours to answer' and 'clean' are different sentences.
A `third-party` disposition takes `not-ours` and nothing else; a `fleet-unlockable` one takes
any of the other three and never `not-ours`. Held by
`lock-pinned-digests.py --check-registry-retention`, on every pull request, with no credential.
Design: Doc/Architecture/FleetRegistryRetention.
🚨 `publishes` IS THE THIRD QUESTION, AND IT IS THE ONE THAT WAS NEVER ASKED (MeshWeaver#4323).
`disposition` says whether this lane can LOCK a host; `retention` says what DELETES from it;
neither asks whether this fleet PUBLISHES there. For a day this file said of `ghcr.io` both
'never published by this fleet' and 'Nothing this fleet produces is stored on ghcr.io' while
`main-cd.yml` pushed twelve tags across three of our own repositories there on every promoting
run — and BOTH fields validated green, because every other arm asks this record what it says
and none asked the WORKFLOWS what they do.
A host this fleet pushes to satisfies the table in one of two ways, and
`--check-registry-retention` DERIVES the push targets from the publishing lanes
(.github/workflows/main-cd.yml and release.yml — every `--tag` argument and every
mirror-image-to-registry.sh destination, shell continuations joined) rather than reading them
here:
disposition: fleet-unlockable   the host-level declaration already says our images live
there, and its `retention` block already has to say what
keeps them. Nothing further is required (cr.meshweaver.cloud).
a `publishes` block             for a MIXED host, where the disposition is about what the
fleet pulls. Requires `repositories` (checked for EQUALITY
against the derived set, both ways — a missing one is the
gap, a stale one hides the next), `producedBy` (lanes that
exist AND mention the host), `runFrom` (whether any
installation runs from them) and a `retention` block whose
rule is `operator-retained`: the store's operator keeps them
and this fleet does not. That rule may NOT carry `deleters`
— we cannot measure somebody else's deletion mechanisms from
a committed file, so the list would be a verdict about OUR
artifacts resting on nothing — and may not authorize a
cleanup. It is deliberately NOT a host-level rule: allowing
it there would be a trapdoor out of `nothing-deletes`.
🚨 AND AN OVERLAY MAY NOT PIN A PUBLISHED REPOSITORY. That is what stops `publishes` being
prose: an installation pinning `<host>/<a published repo>` is running OUR images from a store
nothing of ours retains and this lane cannot lock, and the host's `third-party` disposition
would wave it through in the one branch — pins here AND there — that prints success. It fires
on nobody today, which is exactly the claim `publishes.runFrom` makes.
🚨 WHY THE DISPOSITION WAS NOT SIMPLY FLIPPED. `third-party` → `fleet-unlockable` on `ghcr.io`
is the correct-sounding fix and it REDS THE LANE: `memex-cloud` pins its portal and migration
images in this ACR AND `ghcr.io/distribution/distribution` (the registry service's own image,
which cannot come from the registry it boots), so the flip makes `resolve_running_sets` fire
'half its running set would be protected and half would not' over an installation whose every
image OF OURS is here and protected. `pause.reEnableWhen` is 'lock-pinned-digests is green',
so that false red would stand between the fleet and re-enabling cleanup. The unit is the
problem, not the value: one disposition per host is false about one half of a mixed host
whichever way it reads.
Removing an entry is how an installation re-enters the expected set.
An installation that is LIVE but not reachable from a GitHub-hosted runner is deliberately
NOT a state here. It would be an exemption meaning `this one never has to answer`, which is
the shape that goes stale silently — and the two installations measured on 2026-09-12 both
answer over the public internet. If one ever cannot, that is a decision to take then, in a
reviewed diff, and it needs its own state rather than being filed under `retired`.
🚨 AN INSTALLATION'S IDENTITY IS `owner/name:id`, NOT `id` (MeshWeaver#3438, 2026-09-15).
`Hosting__Deployment` is unique inside ONE deployments repository and inside nothing larger.
A client's deployments repository joined the fleet on 2026-09-14 and its instance was then
`memex` too (HISTORY — it has since been renamed) — correctly, inside that repository — and the
collision took this lane down the same night with `installation 'memex' is declared by two
overlays … so which host answers for it is ambiguous`. NEITHER installation was then asked
anything, so `memex` — the one actually exposed to the ACR purge — got no locks either, and
the red sat on `pause.reEnableWhen`. An entry below may therefore carry `repo`, and it MUST
where two repositories declare the same id: an unqualified line would otherwise exempt an
installation nobody wrote it about. The duplicate blocker still fires for one repository
declaring an id in two overlays — which is what it was always about.
🚨 `repositories` (below) IS THE HALF THAT STOPS THAT QUALIFICATION BECOMING AN EXEMPTION.
Keying by repository is what lets two repositories each declare a `memex`; on its own it also
means a new deployments repository joins the fleet SILENTLY, its installations becoming their
own slots with nobody having read a line about them — 'a fork reds the lane' traded for 'a
fork is invisible to it', the same defect in the other costume. So every repository whose tree
carries deployment overlay FILES is named there, checked BOTH ways: an undeclared one is a
blocker, and a name no repository answers to is a stale line that hides the next one. The
population is overlay FILES rather than extracted installations on purpose — a repository
whose overlays this reader stopped understanding would otherwise vanish from the table's reach
exactly when that mattered.
🚨 A CLIENT ESTATE IS NOT DECLARED IN THIS FILE. This repository is public, and a client's
deployments repository, registry and installations are the client's identity. Their lines live
in a private source and reach the lane through the ACR_RETENTION_PRIVATE_ROSTER secret (env
MW_ACR_PRIVATE_ROSTER): a JSON document of this file's shape, merged over it by
lock-pinned-digests.py's read_roster_document, where a key declared in both is a refusal. Without
the secret (a fork, a local run) the committed fleet is all there is, and a client repository the
scan reaches is an UNDECLARED repository — red, as it should be.

Systemorph/Memex.reason: The fleet's deployments repository: the AKS overlays for every installation Systemorph operates (measured 2026-09-15: 8 overlay files). Its overlays are AXIS 2's tag pins and AXIS 3's expected-installation denominator.

Systemorph/MeshWeaver.Deploy.reason: The PUBLIC deployment reference that received this repository's deploy material (MeshWeaver.Deploy#1-#3, MeshWeaver#7158): the portal Helm chart (`deploy/helm`), the per-instance PostgreSQL chart (`deploy/helm-db`), an EXAMPLE AKS overlay with the cluster manifests and the chart / drift / observability tooling (`deploy/aks`), memex-local, and the chart guards. Since core slimming it also carries the four opt-in SERVICE charts that left this repository (`deploy/{s1-extract,whisper,ocr,ollama}/helm`, each a `values.yaml` that matches the overlay path filter and declares no installation) — so this repository's own entry was removed with them: core's tree carries no overlay file any more, and `--self-test` ARM 35 pins that the table names this repository exactly when it does. Its README states the scope: defaults, placeholders and example values only — an installation's own values live in its operator's private deployments repository, never there. Measured 2026-10-25 over its `main` tree (untruncated): the lane counts 45 files matching the overlay path filter — chart values, `values.*.example.yaml` and `deploy/aks/scripts/testdata/values.*.yaml` render fixtures — and NOT ONE declares an installation (`deploy/helm/values.yaml` sets no `Hosting__Deployment`; the example AKS overlay's host is `portal.example.com`), so it yields nothing on AXIS 3. Its chart defaults pin `ghcr.io/systemorph/memex-portal-ai:latest` and `memex-migration:latest` exactly as this repository's `deploy/helm/values.yaml` does, which the lane reports as `published by us` rather than as a running set. Named here for the same reason as `Systemorph/MeshWeaver`: a repository that contributes pin sites and is absent from the table is the silent one this table exists to refuse. The day it gains a real installation's overlay, that is a client or operator estate in a public repository and is itself the defect.

cr.meshweaver.cloud.reason: The fleet's OWN container registry, hosted by MeshWeaver (MeshWeaver#3697) and the default for newly provisioned instances. `acr purge` cannot reach it and this lane cannot lock a manifest there, so an installation running from it is out of THIS lane's scope. 🚨 THAT IS STILL NOT A CLAIM THAT THIS LANE PROTECTS IT — the out-of-scope report line says UNVERIFIED and must keep saying it. What keeps or deletes images there is answered in the `retention` block below rather than by this field: ONE governed cleanup may delete manifests, only the complement of a protected set it derives on every run, and it is not yet authorized to (MeshWeaver#4230, MeshWeaver#7530, Doc/Architecture/FleetRegistryRetention). Measured 2026-09-13: 4 references across the fleet's overlays (two installations, two each), which the nightly run now PRINTS as that registry's protected-set floor.

authorizationBlockedBy: Blob garbage-collection is not built (MeshWeaver.Plugins#4370 slice 3): a manifest DELETE frees no storage until it is, so a real run cannot yet meet this issue's cost acceptance.
A migration Job outside any instance action (a hand-run `helm upgrade`) is not seen by the derivation (MeshWeaver.Plugins#4370 slice 4).

Tag writers outside instance actions do not respect the lease: core's release.yml promotion retag, the CD publish that moves `latest`/`main`, and a hand or rollback retag can attach a tag to a planned digest after the run's last re-read of it (manual `Hosting/FleetRegistryCleanup` → Still open).

The control instance holds no publisher credential yet (`Hosting:FleetRegistry:Host`, `TokenRealm`, `PublisherPassword`): the one what-if, Ops/Actions/fleet-registry-cleanup-whatif-20261101-7530 on the control instance, read 0 manifests and refused (R1) naming `no trusted registry host is configured`. Setting it is the owner's.
The first deleting run is the owner's to approve, against a what-if that read the whole registry with no refusal.
retention.reason: Restated over MeshWeaver.Plugins main, read-only: a cleanup now EXISTS, so `nothing-deletes` stopped being true the day MeshWeaver.Plugins#4878 merged — the explicit-DELETE row below names it. What did NOT change is R1: `distribution` has no lock, the derivation is the whole safety margin, and every axis refuses on an incomplete reading. The one run so far proves the refusal, not the deletion: Ops/Actions/fleet-registry-cleanup-whatif-20261101-7530 on the control instance found two consumers unreadable and no registry credential, read 0 manifests, and marked nothing deletable. `cleanupAuthorized` therefore stays false, and `authorizationBlockedBy` names what it waits for.

cleanup.governedBy: Hosting/InstanceAction on the control instance: what-if by default; a deleting run parks for ONE approval bound to the exact digests, holds the registry-maintenance lease (MeshWeaver.Plugins#4852), revalidates before each DELETE and verifies by digest (MeshWeaver.Plugins#4878).
cleanup.deletes: manifests by digest (and with them every tag naming them). Never a blob: that is the GC row.

axes.derivedFrom: every ImageClosure node under Admin/ImageClosures, read as System — every CD-published image has one, so this is the newest sealed set and every older one
every Hosting/Deployment record's pinnedImageTag, partitions:all, as System — the chart renders portal.image and migration.image from it, so it is the committed pin
each live installation's own Hosting/DeploymentStatus sample (per pod, current, scraped, replicaCountsComplete and livePodsComplete) — read from the instance, never from its record
every Hosting/InstanceAction, partitions:all: an in-flight or Unobserved Roll/Provision protects its target tag; any other in-flight image-applying kind refuses the run
the registry's own tag listing: every clean <major>.<minor>.0 tag, latest, main, stable and the -latest pointers
the manifest bodies of every kept index, level by level, tagged or not
none can be derived yet (R6), so every repository under plugins/ is protected wholesale

deleters.verdict: ENABLED — age 168h, interval 24h, dryrun false. The one automatic deletion in this registry, and it reaches INCOMPLETE UPLOAD SESSIONS only (the `_uploads/` scratch state of a push that never finished). It can never reach a manifest, a tag or a referenced blob. 🚨 PROVENANCE: the KEY and its window are read off the committed chart; what the key DELETES is distribution's own documented behaviour, not something measured here — it is an off-the-shelf component we render rather than extend. It is the one row a distribution major version could change without any file in this repo moving, which is why both images are pinned BY DIGEST; a bump is the moment to re-read it.

No Job, no CronJob — the 8 objects rendered under deploy/helm/templates/registry are 2 ConfigMaps, 2 Deployments, 2 Services, an Ingress and a SecretProviderClass — and no invocation anywhere in deploy/ or .github/ (hand sweep 2026-09-14 over all 409 files under deploy/ and .github/; the GATE sweeps the 246 of them that can run a command and names the 3 it skips — two denominators, not one. Both with the pattern proven on a synthetic control first). So blobs are never collected: this is the unbounded-growth half. 🚨 STILL TRUE AFTER MeshWeaver#7530: the named cleanup deletes MANIFESTS only, so until GC runs a deletion frees no storage. GC inside a read-only window, run by the same governed action under the lease, is MeshWeaver.Plugins#4370 slice 3; when it lands this row becomes `present: true` with `governedBy: FleetRegistryCleanup`, and a Job or CronJob in the chart still reds.

deleters.mechanism: an explicit registry DELETE (HTTP DELETE, or a crane / skopeo / regctl / oras / az-acr-repository deletion)
deleters.verdict: PRESENT, and it is the ONE deleter this record accepts: the `FleetRegistryCleanup` kind of `Hosting/InstanceAction` (MeshWeaver.Plugins `Hosting/InstanceAction`, manual `Hosting/FleetRegistryCleanup`; the delete path landed in MeshWeaver.Plugins#4878 under the lease of #4852). It sends `DELETE /v2/<repo>/manifests/<digest>` as the publisher, only on a request with `registryCleanupExecute: true`, after ONE approval bound to exactly the digests it deletes, while holding the registry-maintenance lease that every image-applying instance action is refused by, and it revalidates the protected set after the inventory and before EACH DELETE. A what-if (the default) has no write. Everything ELSE in this row is unchanged: core's sweep over `deploy/` and `.github/` still finds zero callers, and CD only ever PUSHES — so a DELETE anywhere in this repository is still RED, because only the named job is accepted.

Refused by the ACL, not by a grep: docker_auth grants the `delete` action to EXACTLY ONE account, the publisher. Every other authenticated account matches a pull-only rule and anonymous matches no rule at all, so an installation holding an instance key cannot delete whatever it asks. The named cleanup runs AS that publisher account (`cleanup.runsAs`), and the gate reds if the two ever differ.

deleters.mechanism: acr purge / the two recorded ACR tasks
deleters.verdict: Cannot reach this host — `az acr` addresses meshweaver.azurecr.io. This is the fact that makes MeshWeaver#4230 a separate question from MeshWeaver#3438 rather than a restatement of it.

deleters.mechanism: an Azure blob lifecycle / management policy on the registry's storage container
deleters.verdict: MEASURED ABSENT on 2026-10-11, in production, through the governed read: the `RegistryRetention` dry run on the control instance (request Ops/Actions/registry-retention-verify-20261011-3438, operations-lane run 38141799080) read the management policy of the storage account the committed records name (`meshweaverregistry`) as the operator identity and printed `registry_lifecycle=meshweaverregistry present=false`. The lane derives that from Azure's own `ManagementPolicyNotFound` answer, never from an exit code, and a read it could not make is a red run naming the account — so this is a measured absence, not a refusal read as one. 🚨 It is a reading at a DATE, not a property of the chart: the account is provisioned outside it, so no committed file re-derives this row. Every `RegistryRetention` verify re-takes it and prints the same line; a `present=true` there makes this row false, and it is then corrected to `true` with the policy quoted. A lifecycle rule over a CONTENT-ADDRESSED store is not old data expiring — it deletes a layer a current manifest still names — which is why policy `fleet-registry-bounded` forbids using one as the cleanup. `cleanupAuthorized` stays false: what it waits for now is the cleanup that derives its protected set (MeshWeaver#6499), not this row.
deleters.measuredBy: The governed `RegistryRetention` InstanceAction with `dryRun: true` on the control instance (MeshWeaver.Plugins Hosting/InstanceAction; lane step in the estate's operations workflow). Unattended, read-only, no approval. Doc/Architecture/FleetRegistryRetention section 7.

ghcr.io.reason: 🚨 THE ONLY MIXED HOST IN THE FLEET, and the `disposition` is about what the fleet PULLS — which is what every axis reads it for. What the fleet's overlays PIN here is somebody else's and was never ours to protect: `ghcr.io/distribution/distribution` and `ghcr.io/oras-project/oras` (the registry service's own image and the bundle-pull helper, both pulled from outside precisely because a registry cannot serve the image that boots it), plus one line of PROSE in the ci-runners overlay describing what the runner image is built from — which is why whole-line comments are stripped before extraction. What this fleet PUBLISHES here is OURS, it is a different set of repositories, and it is declared in `publishes` below rather than by this field. 🚨 A SINGLE PER-HOST DISPOSITION IS FALSE ABOUT ONE HALF WHICHEVER VALUE IT TAKES, and both halves are measured: `third-party` read as a claim about the whole host was false about `systemorph/*` (MeshWeaver#4323, the reason this entry was rewritten), and `fleet-unlockable` is false about `distribution/*` AND REDS THE LANE — `memex-cloud` pins `meshweaver.azurecr.io/memex-portal-ai:3.0.0-ci.8411` AND `ghcr.io/distribution/distribution:3.1.1`, so flipping the host makes `resolve_running_sets` fire 'half its running set would be protected and half would not' over an installation whose every image OF OURS is in this ACR and protected. `pause.reEnableWhen` is 'lock-pinned-digests is green', so that false red would stand between the fleet and re-enabling cleanup.

publishes.runFrom: NO INSTALLATION. Measured 2026-09-15 over the fleet's deployment overlays: not one names a `ghcr.io/systemorph/*` image. The only committed `systemorph/*` references on this host are the CHART'S OWN DEFAULTS (deploy/helm/values.yaml `portal.image` and `migration.image`, both `:latest`), and that file declares `Hosting__Deployment: ""` — it is the chart's default value set, not an installation, so it yields no instance on AXIS 3. 🚨 THAT IS WHAT MAKES THIS A PUBLICATION AND NOT A SOURCE THIS LANE MUST PROTECT, and it is also the thing most likely to stop being true: an overlay that ever pins one of these repositories is running our images from a store nothing of ours retains and this lane cannot lock, so `classify_foreign_registries` REDS on it by name rather than letting it pass as a third-party pin. The chart defaults themselves are MeshWeaver#4323's open half — an unconfigured install pulls the platform from here, at a moving tag.

retention.reason: Measured 2026-09-15, read-only: our images ARE stored here and their retention is GITHUB'S, not this fleet's. Nothing of ours deletes from ghcr.io — the deleter sweep over `deploy/` and `.github/` finds no deletion against this host, and CD only ever PUSHES — and nothing of ours CAN lock here: `changeableAttributes.deleteEnabled` is an ACR feature. 🚨 THE DIFFERENCE FROM `nothing-deletes` IS THAT WE CANNOT SHOW IT, and that is why this rule exists rather than reusing that one. A `nothing-deletes` enumeration is held to a COMMITTED CHART the gate re-derives the deleters from, plus the ACL that carries the `delete` action; GitHub Packages is rendered by no file of ours and its ACL is not ours to read, so an enumeration here would be a verdict about our artifacts resting on nothing — the same false reassurance `not-ours` refuses one field along. What IS established: this is a MIRROR, never an origin. Every reference is copied by digest from `meshweaver.azurecr.io` (main-cd Phase B/D and release.yml's mirror step, all `docker buildx imagetools create`, never a second build), the ACR copy is the one this lane locks, and `cr.meshweaver.cloud` carries the same set for the installations that actually run from a registry. So a GHCR retention event loses a MIRROR of an image that exists, protected, in two other registries. The consumer that would notice is MeshWeaver.Plugins, which pins `ghcr.io/systemorph/mw-plugin-test:latest` as MW_TEST_IMAGE.

Scoped, like the `disposition` beside it, to what this fleet PULLS from ghcr.io — the BOOTSTRAP set: `distribution` and `oras`, images we run and do not produce, pulled from outside precisely because a registry cannot serve the image that boots it. Their retention is GitHub's and they were never ours to protect. 🚨 THIS FIELD SAID `Nothing this fleet produces is stored on ghcr.io` UNTIL 2026-09-15 AND THAT WAS FALSE (MeshWeaver#4323): `main-cd.yml` pushed twelve tags across three of our OWN repositories here on every promoting run — measured in the job log of run 34918214035 at 02:27Z that day — while `release.yml`, the lane the issue named, had never run at all (0 runs). What this fleet produces and stores here is declared in `publishes` above, and `--check-registry-retention` now DERIVES that set from the publishing workflows, so neither field can go false again without reddening.

instances.reason: The fleet's build server (build.meshweaver.cloud, MeshWeaver.Plugins#1784). It is LIVE and it ANSWERS — the 2026-09-13 01:18Z run read core c84c6c0 from it — but deployments/aks/build/values.build.public.yaml pins `cr.meshweaver.cloud/memex-portal-ai:3.0.0-ci.8411` and its migration twin in the FLEET'S OWN registry, which `acr purge` cannot reach and this lane cannot lock. Before the `registries` table above existed, the ACR-scoped extractor read that overlay as pinning ZERO and the run refused with `pins no image at all` — a false sentence that reddened the lane on the 2026-09-12 and 2026-09-13 schedules (the last successful apply run was 2026-09-11T01:13Z) and, because `pause.reEnableWhen` is `lock-pinned-digests is green`, stood between the fleet and re-enabling cleanup. 🚨 THIS ENTRY DECLARES NOTHING AND EXEMPTS NOTHING — `build` is `live` and is expected to answer like any other. The registry declaration is in the `registries` table ABOVE, and what retains cr.meshweaver.cloud is established by nothing and tracked on MeshWeaver#3438. This line is here so that the day `build` is decommissioned, the state is changed rather than discovered.
